claims.claim: Politics, as a social institution, is the system through which societies make collective decisions and allocate power. Sociologically, a society's political structure and practices provide insight into the distribution of power and wealth, and politics is studied as the interaction between citizens and their government — who gets to make decisions and who holds power.
Power is the ability to exercise one's will over others (Max Weber, 1922); it shapes personal relationships, social groups, professional organizations, and governments alike.

Authority is accepted power — power that people agree to follow. The state is a political organization of society, or the body politic, whose purpose is to establish order and security using laws enforced within its jurisdiction or geographic boundaries.

A democracy is a form of government that strives to provide all citizens with an equal voice, or vote, in determining state policy; in democracies citizens are free to organize political parties and hold elections, and elected leaders are bound by the nation's constitution and limited in the powers they can exercise.

A monarchy is a government in which a single person (a monarch) rules until he or she dies or abdicates the throne, with the title usually claimed by hereditary succession or divine appointment; modern monarchies are often constitutional, with the monarch bound by a constitution while elected leaders govern.

In a dictatorship — the most direct form of concentrated authoritarian rule — power is held by a single person or a very small group that wields complete and absolute authority over the government and population, with no accountability to an electorate.

Political participation takes many forms: voting (in any given U.S. election year roughly half the population does not vote), organizing (democracies guarantee citizens the freedom to organize political parties and other groups), and protesting (documented nonviolent protest strategies include rallies, sit-ins, marches, petitions, and boycotts, used by leaders such as Mohandas Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr.).

People acquire political beliefs and habits through the ordinary agents of socialization — the family, schools, mass media, and government are documented agents — so political socialization happens largely through family, school, and media.

Power is distributed unequally: societies' political structures and practices reveal the distribution of power and wealth, and observers have noted that small, well-connected groups can exert influence far out of proportion to their numbers — a factual observation, not a policy position.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How evenly is power actually shared in democracies?
positions: Democratic ideals hold that citizens exercise an equal voice or vote in determining state policy, with citizens free to organize parties and hold elections (OpenStax 17.2).

Empirical observations complicate the ideal: voter turnout is limited (roughly half the U.S. population does not vote in a given election year), and commentators have argued that wealthy, well-connected minorities exert outsized influence — some have labeled even the United States an oligarchy (OpenStax 17.2, 17.3).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states both honestly without taking sides: the systems are described factually (democracy's equal-voice ideal; authoritarianism's concentration of power), and the honest note is a factual observation — power is distributed unequally — with no policy prescription and no endorsement of any position. The lesson's scenarios are original and fictional.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft in public/content/phase-4/lessons.json contained no definition of politics, no sources, and no power-and-arrangements content; its claims ('Politics is a foundational concept in Sociology', 'a label on a toolbox drawer', 'Like reading a map legend') were generic boilerplate with no source support and were discarded entirely.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced all boilerplate with source-verified content: working definition of politics as the system through which societies make collective decisions and allocate power, attributed to OpenStax Introduction to Sociology 3e chapter 17; power (Weber 1922, via OpenStax 17.1); authority as accepted power; the state as the organized political body (Britannica); democracy, authoritarianism/dictatorship, and monarchy described factually with one line each (OpenStax 17.2); political participation (voting, organizing, protesting) with attributed facts (OpenStax 17.1, 17.2, 17.3); political socialization via family, school, and media (OpenStax 5.3); the honest note (unequal distribution of power) stated factually with no policy position. All examples are original and fictional.

Supports only the political-socialization line: people learn to function in their social worlds through agents of socialization, with the family as the first agent, formal institutions (schools, workplaces, government) teaching people how to behave in and navigate systems, and mass media distributing information to a wide audience and influencing norms. Used to ground the claim that political beliefs and habits are learned mainly through family, school, and media. General socialization itself is the sibling topic sociology:foundations:socialization.
